checkpoints.question: What is the primary function of a mantrap vestibule in physical security?

options.A: It records video of all people entering the facility for later review
options.B: It alerts security staff when an unauthorized person attempts entry
options.C: It physically prevents tailgating by admitting only one person at a time
options.D: It requires all visitors to scan an ID badge before proceeding

checkpoints.explanation: A mantrap vestibule is a double-door airlock that blocks tailgating mechanically, regardless of social pressure or badge status — it is a physical control, not a detection or monitoring system.

checkpoints.question: Explain the difference between what a standard ATM skimmer captures and what a shimmer device captures.
checkpoints.rubric: A sound answer states that a skimmer captures magnetic stripe data (via overlay on the card slot), while a shimmer is inserted inside the chip slot and captures chip data — and that shimmer data enables card-not-present fraud because no physical chip is needed for online purchases.
checkpoints.explanation: The section explicitly states that an ATM skimmer overlay reads the magnetic stripe, while a shimmer device reads chip data and enables card-not-present fraud where no physical chip is required.

checkpoints.question: Why does cloning a contactless payment card fail to complete a transaction, but cloning an HID proximity badge succeeds in granting access?

options.A: Payment cards require biometric confirmation, while badges only need the card ID
options.B: Payment cards use dynamic cryptograms per transaction, while proximity badges broadcast a static ID
options.C: Payment cards are encrypted end-to-end, while badges transmit in plaintext
options.D: Payment cards use multi-factor authentication, while badges use single-factor only

checkpoints.explanation: The section states that contactless payment cards generate a dynamic cryptogram (one-time code) per transaction, so a static clone cannot work; older cards lack this protection and remain vulnerable.

checkpoints.question: Why do USB Rubber Ducky and O.MG Cable attacks bypass both antivirus and application allowlisting?
checkpoints.rubric: A sound answer states that these devices emulate a keyboard and fire pre-programmed keystrokes, invoking legitimate OS utilities (like PowerShell) by typing commands — no malicious file is written to disk, so antivirus and allowlisting (which control files and programs) do not detect or block them.
checkpoints.explanation: The section explicitly notes that these attacks bypass antivirus and allowlisting because they invoke legitimate utilities through keystroke injection, not file execution or program launch.

checkpoints.question: Which defense prevents data theft at a compromised public USB charging station while still allowing the device to charge?

options.A: A password prompt on the charging device
options.B: A VPN connection active during charging
options.C: An antivirus scan before connecting to the station
options.D: A power-only USB cable with data lines physically absent

checkpoints.explanation: A power-only USB cable has no data lines, so it cannot carry stolen data to or from the charging station — power still flows to the device.

checkpoints.question: Why is full disk encryption alone insufficient to prevent a cold boot attack?
checkpoints.rubric: A sound answer states that encryption keys are stored in DRAM while the system is powered on, and DRAM retains its contents for seconds to minutes after power is cut — so an attacker can recover the keys from RAM before they are erased, even if the stored disk data is encrypted.
checkpoints.explanation: The section explains that DRAM retains contents after power-off and that full disk encryption protects stored data but not keys already loaded in RAM, which a cold boot attack targets directly.

checkpoints.question: Which of the following is a defense against hardware implants?

options.A: Tamper-evident chassis seals and hardware chain of custody
options.B: Frequent patching of the operating system
options.C: Strong passwords on all user accounts
options.D: Regular antivirus scans of the hard drive

checkpoints.explanation: The section lists tamper-evident seals and chain of custody as defenses; antivirus, passwords, and OS patches operate at the software level and do not detect or prevent hardware implants below the OS.

checkpoints.question: Which of the following is an example of an environmental attack?

options.A: Cutting external electrical panels to cause a facility-wide power outage
options.B: Sending a phishing email to trick an employee into revealing credentials
options.C: Installing malware on a web server to steal customer data
options.D: Exploiting a buffer overflow vulnerability in application code

checkpoints.explanation: Environmental attacks target infrastructure that computing equipment depends on — power, cooling, fire suppression, and plumbing — not the equipment itself; the other options are software or network attacks.
